title: An implemented decision note says the SQLite session backend is absent while the package exists, the CLI depends on it and the subsystem page lists it
The cross-process write lease and the Windows binding are copied into both session backends instead of shared

reason: The service-plus-handle contract is kept as a Go contract package with a conformance suite; readers and writers become two interface types and no listener routes events into storage.

Per-session files with generations, Zstandard frames, torn-tail recovery and exclusive publication are replaced by one SQLite database whose transactions give the same guarantees; the readable one-file-per-session artifact survives as the export.

The package exists at the pinned commit as an optional provider. Its WAL mode, group commit with savepoints, append-only triggers and identity pragmas are carried into the one Go store; its 64-event frames, linked segments and import of JSONL on first open are not.

The stage machinery exists only to run a chain of adjacent format migrations over old files. The Go store reads only its own format and evolves each event type by a payload version, so there is no chain to run.
The build-time catalogue of codecs and migration edges exists only to keep formats 0 to 3 readable. No Go package reads an upstream format generation in the store's read path.
A frozen reader of upstream format 0 and its edge to format 1. Formats 0 to 3 are never read by the Go harness; their holders upgrade them with upstream first.
A migration edge that folds stream chunks and renumbers every event of an upstream format 1 file. Formats 0 to 3 are never read by the Go harness, and the Go store never renumbers.
A migration edge that moves the system prompt into events and renumbers an upstream format 2 file. Formats 0 to 3 are never read by the Go harness.
The edge from format 3 to 4 is not built. The package also holds the format 4 codec; the deferred import command specifies its own reader for format 4 files and is not a port of this package.

The three durability checkpoints (before a model attempt, before a top-level tool body, at each step boundary) and the fail-closed rule are kept as checkpoint.Policy, called by the driver and the tool pipeline at the three points, failing closed; with no policy mounted the callers flush directly.
The bounded incremental upload with an acceptance watermark is kept as a component, but it is off until the user opts in and obeys the one off-switch, which reverses upstream's default.
The Go checkpoint policy also records the intent to run a tool, not the completion of its external effect.
justification: No local mechanism can observe whether an external effect completed. The call id is handed to every tool body as an idempotency key and recovery reports the outcome as unknown. Stage DH-S-0 is a placeholder until the implementation plan assigns the stage of DH-D-STORE-4.

reason: The Go design also places no checkpoint inside a running model attempt, so a crash loses stream frames that had not settled.
justification: Logging every stream chunk would put a disk sync in the stream path. Nothing model-visible is lost because the attempt never settled; the user loses text that was on screen. Stage DH-S-0 is a placeholder until the implementation plan assigns the stage of DH-D-STORE-4.

reason: The Go design also records a tool call without a result as outcome unknown and never retries it automatically.
justification: Kept on purpose: retrying a call that may already have taken effect is the worse error, so the model is told to verify. Stage DH-S-0 is a placeholder until the implementation plan assigns the stage of DH-D-STORE-4.

reason: There is no catalogue of format migrations to own or distribute: upcasters are registered together with their event type in first-party Go code.
No historical chain exists whose missing edge a plugin would need to supply; a payload version without its upcaster fails the recorded-row test at build time.
The Go store never converts a stored row, so an unknown ignorable record is kept byte for byte and nothing is refused for it. Only the upstream importer keeps the strict refusal, deliberately.
No adjacent edges and no successor files exist in the Go store, so nothing has to select later migrations or publish a result.
The Go store never converts a stored row, so an unknown ignorable record is kept byte for byte and nothing is refused for it. Only the upstream importer keeps the strict refusal, deliberately.
The Go store never renumbers events, so no sequence remap table grows with the log; reads are paged windows from the database.

No generations exist, so there is no retained predecessor that could be mistaken for a fallback. The Go rule for its own layout is forward-only migration after an automatic backup, which is the rollback.
The ambiguity of the old preset id exists only in upstream format 2 files, which the Go harness never reads.
No committed generations and no settings file are migrated: the Go store has one database whose layout is migrated in one transaction after a backup.
The store has no converter whose coverage could be incomplete. The importer reads only files already at format 4 and refuses a whole file it cannot map, writing nothing.
There is no whole-log format version to finalise or protect by a checkpoint record: each event type evolves alone, guarded by the persisted-type inventory test.
No future whole-log format needs prerequisite readers of an earlier one: an older payload version is read through its registered upcaster, and a recorded row for every version must keep decoding.
The refusal of nested historical tool-result wrappers belongs to a migration edge the Go design does not have. The importer accepts only format 4 files and refuses what its table cannot map.
The Go store has no prefixed historical extension fields. The importer maps an extension field it knows and refuses a file that carries one it does not, so none is kept without a consumer.

In the Go store a parent and its child sessions are rows of one database linked by a column, so no fact has to be recovered from child files. The importer imports a root as a whole and reports children it did not find.

Unknown historical child modes arise only when a migration reconstructs a parent catalogue from old files. The Go store reconstructs nothing; the importer carries an entry as recorded or refuses the file.
There is one store per harness home and no per-root migration scope. Bringing sessions in from elsewhere is the export and import pair, and upstream roots enter through the importer.
No migration returns a whole current history: the store serves paged windows from the database and projections open from checkpoints.
Whole-log adjacent integer versions are replaced by a payload version per event type with upcasters on read, so one type changes without touching any other event.
An upload acknowledged just before a crash can still be sent again in the Go design, because the acknowledgement arrives over HTTP before the acceptance record is durable.
justification: At-least-once is inherent to an acknowledgement over HTTP. The window is narrowed: the acceptance record is committed as soon as the writer is free, and each event carries session id and seq so a receiver can remove duplicates. Stage DH-S-0 is a placeholder until the implementation plan assigns the stage of DH-D-STORE-9.

reason: The Go contract states the meaning of absence: a request that is not attributed to a session this process holds carries no field and records nothing, and a test asserts it.
In the Go design one event larger than the byte limit still blocks the upload behind it until the limit is raised.
justification: Skipping the event would leave a gap in a log the receiver expects to be contiguous. The block is made visible: the settings page shows the blocking event and its size. Stage DH-S-0 is a placeholder until the implementation plan assigns the stage of DH-D-STORE-9.

reason: A rejection opens a per-session breaker: the uploader stops attaching the field and reports it, and the attempt is retried without extension fields, so an optional field cannot keep failing model requests. It needs the adapter of area A04.
The Go store has one database with no per-root encoding and no catalogued chain of generations, so there is nothing whose encoding a migration must preserve.
There are no file layouts, old or new: sessions are rows, and upstream's pre-release flat layout is never read.
The export is one header line and one line per event, optionally gzip, readable by ordinary tools; the database itself is stock SQLite.
The store has a delete operation that removes a session's events, checkpoints, index rows and blob references, and an optional retention duty.

Ownership is an epoch checked inside every append transaction, so an explicit takeover from a stuck holder is safe and a removed lock file cannot corrupt a log. The Windows lock is a file lock, not a name scoped to a login session, and a home on a network filesystem is refused.
The cordis change that makes unload complete and ordered removes the cause; the store additionally stops admitting appends and runs one bounded final barrier before it releases its leases.
No file is published by hard link or rename: a session comes into existence by a transaction that inserts its row, and a second insert of the same id fails on the key.
Exists only because Node has no file-lock call and needs a prebuilt native add-on; Go reaches flock and LockFileEx through golang.org/x/sys without a native build.
Nothing is imported when a session is opened, so a read open has no hidden write of legacy history. Import is an explicit command.

There is no second live store beside the database. The importer is one-way by the owner's decision, records where a session came from and leaves the upstream files untouched, so nothing presents them as a current copy.
Every dsh process uses the one store, and the lease in its session rows excludes a second writer whichever process it is.
A change to an event type raises that type's payload version and adds an upcaster applied on read; stored rows stay as written, so no history migration of the database is needed.
Cross-process write ownership is part of the store contract, not a provider detail: the lease is specified once and the conformance tests include two-process cases.
The store is a service that sessions depend on, so they unload first and close their writers in order, and the store has no option whose change needs a reload under live sessions.

No listener path exists that could be absent: events reach storage only through the writer a session holds, so a session without a writer cannot be mistaken for a persisted one. Area A01 confirms the constructor.
Delete and retention are operations of the store contract.
Listing is a filtered, keyset-paged query on indexed columns of the session rows and never reads events.
In the Go design an interrupted turn is likewise closed with synthetic closers and never continued.
justification: Kept on purpose: continuing would repeat a model request whose stream is lost and tools whose outcome is unknown. Stage DH-S-0 is a placeholder until the implementation plan assigns the stage of DH-D-STORE-4.

reason: The Go contract defines the result for a request without a held session: no field is attached and no acceptance is recorded, which a test asserts.
The writer commits whenever batches are queued, without a batching window, so the acceptance record becomes durable at once and no separate lightweight checkpoint is needed.
The Go design has one store, and its persisted-type catalogue is generated from the running registry, so a hand-written note cannot disagree with what the code ships.
There is one store and therefore one implementation of the lease and of the platform lock calls.

title: One contract package with typed readers and writers; the store returns the log as written
One row per event, the payload in two columns, history protected by the database, forks by copy
Commit on demand with group commit; durable means committed with a full sync
A lease is an epoch in the session row plus one liveness lock file per process
Three version layers, each refusing in a named direction; a version changes only when an older binary would misread
Another process's commits are seen by polling the database's change counter; once-per-home work uses duty leases
Deletion is a tombstone followed by bounded chunks; retention is off by default
The home must be a local filesystem that supports WAL; files are owner-only; no encryption at rest
The export file is the portable form: raw payload bytes, its own format number, gzip
Session-log upload is an opt-in component, and its acceptance record stays a logged event
Upstream sessions enter only through a separate command that refuses whole files
A request table hands a log-only change to the process that holds the session
A store contract with a conformance suite and an in-memory reference
The SQLite store: one database per home with atomic appends, a flush barrier, paged reads and listing
One writer per session across processes, with safe takeover
Durability checkpoints, honest crash recovery and a bounded shutdown
Each event type evolves by itself, and a persisted type cannot change by accident
Sessions can be deleted, old ones retired, and the store checked and rebuilt
A session can be exported to one readable file and imported back
A process can follow a session another process writes, and once-per-home jobs have one runner
Session-log upload to the vendor, only for a user who opted in
A deferred one-way command imports upstream format 4 sessions
A process that does not hold a session can hand its holder a log-only change
The store conformance suite passes on the in-memory store and on the SQLite store
The open sequence refuses foreign, newer and unsupported homes unchanged, and a layout migration backs up first and is blocked by another live instance
An append transaction stores events and blob references together or not at all, derived rows are never ahead of their events, and the database refuses a rewrite of history
Flush returns only after the commit; a failed commit keeps the batch; the backlog is bounded
A process killed in a loop always reopens to a contiguous log that contains the last flushed event
A second writer is refused, a dead holder's lease is taken with a higher epoch, and a stale writer's append writes nothing
The liveness lock survives an open-and-close of the database file, and the lock file can be read by another process
The checkpoint policy is called before a model attempt and a root tool body, flushes, and fails closed also when no policy is mounted
An interrupted turn is closed by the right events as the first durable batch under the new epoch; shutdown drains within its bound
A changed persisted type fails the inventory test; old payload versions decode; newer and unknown ones refuse with a direction; ignorable records stay byte-identical
Deletion is refused while held elsewhere, survives a kill half-way, leaves no row, and spares forks; retention deletes only unheld old sessions
A rebuild reproduces the search index, view rows and checkpoints; its verify option changes nothing; the check finds a damaged session
Export, import, export is byte-identical; a truncated, altered or oversized file is refused with nothing written
A follower receives another process's committed events once and in order without holding a read transaction; a duty has one holder
A fresh home uploads nothing; the off-switch, the byte limit, the watermark, exclusions and the rejection breaker behave as specified
Upstream format 4 fixtures import to the expected events; an unmappable or older file is refused whole with the database unchanged
A filed request is applied once by the holder, survives a holder killed between read and append, expires when nobody applies it, and goes with its session
Budgets: opening and forking a session of more than 100,000 events and listing the heavy-tailed corpus stay inside their budgets, also in the memory-limited rerun
Two real dsh processes share one home: one writer, and safe takeover
A host killed mid-turn recovers honestly
A process that does not hold a session follows it and hands its holder a change
A deleted session leaves nothing behind, and an interrupted deletion finishes
